title: The Case of the Fifth Word

topics.title: Mystery stories: clues, suspects and red herrings

learn.hook: The last gulab jamun has vanished from the fridge. Three suspects, one sticky clue. Ready, detective?
points: 'The Case of the Fifth Word' is a mystery story in which a puzzle is solved by careful observation and logical thinking.
A mystery story usually has: a puzzle or crime, a detective, suspects, clues, at least one false lead, and a final reveal where the solution is explained.

Key words: clue (a sign that helps solve a puzzle), suspect (a person who may be guilty), culprit (the person who actually did it), alibi (proof that a suspect was somewhere else), motive (the reason for doing it), witness (someone who saw something), evidence (facts or objects that show what happened).
A red herring is a misleading clue that points the reader the wrong way.
A good detective separates facts from guesses and checks every clue.

example.q: Read this original mystery: 'The last gulab jamun vanished from the Iyer family's fridge. Grandma said, "I was at the market all evening," and the shopkeeper agreed. Kavya pointed at the cat, but the fridge door was too heavy for a cat to open. Detective Divya then spotted sweet syrup on her brother Ravi's homework book.' Think it through: who is the likely culprit, and what is the red herring?
steps: Grandma has an alibi: the shopkeeper confirms she was at the market.
The cat is suggested, but it could not open the heavy fridge door: that is the red herring.
The syrup on Ravi's book is evidence that links him to the sweet.
So Ravi is the likely culprit.
example.answer: Ravi is the likely culprit. The cat is the red herring.

learn.reallife: Detective stories like the Feluda tales by Satyajit Ray and the Byomkesh Bakshi stories are loved across India because readers try to solve the case before the detective does.

games.title: Detective dictionary
pairs: a sign that helps solve a puzzle
a person who saw what happened

games.title: The gulab jamun case
items: Grandma has an alibi.
The shopkeeper confirms she was at the market all evening.
The cat could easily open the fridge door.
The fridge door was too heavy for a cat to open.
The syrup on Ravi's book is a clue.
It links Ravi to the missing sweet.
Kavya's idea about the cat is a red herring.
It points the investigation the wrong way.
A suspect is always the culprit.
A suspect is only someone who might be guilty. Many suspects turn out to be innocent.
Divya solved the case by looking carefully at evidence.
She noticed the syrup on the homework book.

quiz.q: Read: 'Grandma said, "I was at the market all evening," and the shopkeeper agreed.' What does Grandma have?
quiz.explain: An alibi is proof that a person was somewhere else when the event happened. The shopkeeper confirms it.
quiz.mistake: Confuses alibi with motive

quiz.q: Read: 'Kavya pointed at the cat, but the fridge door was too heavy for a cat to open.' The cat is a ___.
quiz.explain: The cat is a false lead that cannot be true, which makes it a red herring.
quiz.mistake: Accepts the first suggestion without checking it

quiz.q: What is a 'motive'?
quiz.explain: The motive is why someone did it, for example, loving sweets.
quiz.mistake: Confuses motive with alibi or evidence

quiz.q: Which of these is evidence?
options: A guess that Ravi did it
Syrup stains on Ravi's homework book
quiz.explain: Evidence is a real fact or object. Guesses, feelings and rumours are not evidence.
quiz.mistake: Treats opinions as evidence

quiz.q: What usually happens at the end of a mystery story?
options: The solution is revealed and explained
All the suspects are found guilty
quiz.explain: Mysteries end with the reveal, when the detective explains how the clues lead to the answer.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the structure of a mystery story

quiz.q: The person who actually committed the wrongdoing is the ___.
quiz.explain: The culprit is the one who really did it. A suspect only might have done it.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'suspect' and 'culprit' as if they mean the same

quiz.q: Which word means 'to work out a conclusion from clues'?
quiz.explain: To deduce is to reach a conclusion by reasoning. Detectives deduce from clues.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word with the same ending but a different meaning

quiz.q: Which Indian writer created the detective Feluda?
quiz.explain: Satyajit Ray, the famous filmmaker, also wrote the Feluda detective stories.
quiz.mistake: Picks another well-known Indian author

teach.ask: Gappu puts on a tiny detective hat: How does a detective in a mystery story find out who did it?
teach.praise: Elementary, my dear Gappu! The detective checks clues and evidence, tests each suspect's alibi and uses logic.
teach.nudge: What does a detective look for? How do they rule out some suspects?

learn.hook: A secret message is hidden in plain sight. Only a careful reader will find it!
points: An inference is a conclusion you reach from clues in the text plus what you already know. 'Her umbrella dripped on the floor' lets you infer that it was raining.
A deduction follows strictly from facts: if 'All of Class 8B went on the trip' and 'Neha is in 8B' are true, then 'Neha went on the trip' must be true.
Separate a fact (can be checked), an inference (a sensible conclusion from clues) and a guess (no clue supports it).
Read closely: one small word like 'not', 'only', 'all' or 'some' can change the whole meaning.
Codes and hidden messages use patterns, such as the first letter of each line (an acrostic) or one chosen word from each sentence.

example.q: Think it through: Find the hidden place in this note by reading the first letter of each line: 'Look under the mat / In the blue box / Behind the clock / Raju hid it / And then ran / Right back home / Yes, go now!'
steps: Take the first letter of each line: L, I, B, R, A, R, Y.
Check that the word makes sense as a hiding place: it does.

learn.reallife: Doctors infer illnesses from symptoms, and you infer that a friend is upset from their face and silence.

games.title: Fact, inference or guess?
items: The window glass is broken.
A cricket ball lies on the floor near the window.
The ball probably broke the window.
Muddy footprints lead from the playground to the window, so the players likely came from there.
A ghost probably broke the window.
It must have been an alien.

games.title: How a detective reasons
games.prompt: Put the detective's steps in order
items: Observe the scene carefully
Collect the clues
Think of possible explanations
Rule out the ones that don't fit the clues
Reach the conclusion

quiz.q: All the students of Class 8B wore white on Friday. Neha is in Class 8B. What can we deduce?
quiz.explain: If all of 8B wore white and Neha is in 8B, then Neha wore white. Nothing tells us what she likes.
quiz.mistake: Adds ideas the facts do not support

quiz.q: Read: 'Arjun came in with muddy shoes and a wet umbrella.' What can you infer?
quiz.explain: A wet umbrella and mud are clues that point to rain.
quiz.mistake: Makes a guess not supported by the clues

quiz.q: Which of these is a fact rather than an inference?
quiz.explain: What a clock shows can be checked directly, so it is a fact. The others are conclusions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every confident sentence is a fact

quiz.q: Read the first letter of each word to find the hidden word: 'Every Xylophone Is Totally Silent.'
quiz.explain: E-X-I-T-S spells EXITS.
quiz.mistake: Rearranges the letters instead of reading them in order

quiz.q: Some birds in Ravi's garden are parrots. Mithu is a bird in Ravi's garden. What can we say for sure?
options: We cannot be sure whether Mithu is a parrot
quiz.explain: 'Some' does not mean 'all', so Mithu may or may not be a parrot.
quiz.mistake: Treats 'some' as if it meant 'all'

quiz.q: What is an inference?
options: A conclusion from clues and what you already know
A word that means the opposite
quiz.explain: An inference uses evidence and knowledge to reach a sensible conclusion.
quiz.mistake: Thinks inference is the same as guessing

quiz.q: Read: 'The shop opens only on weekdays.' Today is Sunday. What can we deduce?
quiz.explain: Sunday is not a weekday, and the shop opens only on weekdays, so it is closed.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the word 'only'

quiz.q: Read: 'The lights in Meena's room were off, her bag was gone and her shoes were missing from the rack.' The best inference is that Meena ___.
quiz.explain: Her bag and shoes are gone and her room is dark, so she has probably gone out.
quiz.mistake: Uses only one clue instead of all of them

teach.ask: Gappu sees a wet umbrella by the door. He shouts, 'A monster brought it!' How should he think about it instead?
teach.praise: Hehe, no monster! The wet umbrella is a clue, and from it we can infer that it was raining. That's deduction!
teach.nudge: What clue do you see? What sensible conclusion can you draw from it?

topics.title: Modals of deduction: must, might and can't

learn.hook: A detective never says 'I think maybe perhaps...'. She says 'It MUST be him!' or 'It CAN'T be her!' Modals show how sure we are.
points: Modals of deduction show how certain we are about something.
must = almost certain it is true: The ground is wet. It must have rained.
might / may / could = possible, but not sure: He might be at the library.
can't = almost certain it is NOT true: She can't be at home; I just saw her at school.
For the past, use modal + have + past participle: must have taken, might have forgotten, can't have seen.

example.q: Think it through: The cake tin is empty. There are crumbs on Tinku's shirt. His sister was away all day. Complete: 'Tinku ___ eaten the cake. His sister ___ eaten it.'
steps: The crumbs on Tinku's shirt make it almost certain: must have.
His sister was away all day, so it is almost impossible: can't have.
Use have + past participle (eaten) for past deductions.
example.answer: Tinku must have eaten the cake. His sister can't have eaten it.

learn.reallife: We use these every day: 'You must be hungry after the match', 'Mummy might be stuck in traffic', 'That can't be the bus, it's too early'.

games.title: How sure is the speaker?
items: She must be tired after the long trip.
He might come to the party.
That can't be Raju; he is in Delhi.
They may have missed the train.
You must have worked hard for these marks.
It can't have been the cat; the door was shut.
The key could be in the drawer.

items.text: His eyes are red and he keeps yawning. He ___ be sleepy.
I am not sure where Priya is. She ___ be in the canteen.
That ___ be Mr Rao; he left for Chennai this morning.
The road is flooded. It must ___ rained all night.
I can't find my pen. I might have ___ it at school.

quiz.q: 'The streets are wet and people are carrying umbrellas. It ___ have rained.'
quiz.explain: The clues make it almost certain, so we use 'must have'.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'can't' even though the clues point to yes

quiz.q: Which modal shows that something is possible but not certain?
quiz.explain: 'Might' (and may/could) shows possibility.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'must' shows possibility

quiz.q: 'That ___ be Rohan's bicycle; his is red and this one is blue.'
quiz.explain: The colours do not match, so it is almost certainly not his: can't.
quiz.mistake: Does not use the clue that rules Rohan out

quiz.q: Choose the correct past deduction.
quiz.explain: The pattern is modal + have + past participle: must have forgotten.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'has' or 'had' after a modal

quiz.q: 'He might be at the library.' How sure is the speaker?
quiz.explain: 'Might' shows the speaker thinks it is possible but is not sure.
quiz.mistake: Reads 'might' as a strong certainty

quiz.q: The detective said, 'The thief must have climbed the wall.' This means the detective is ___.
quiz.explain: 'Must have' shows a strong, almost certain deduction about the past.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'must' only means a rule or duty here

quiz.q: Which sentence uses a modal of deduction?
options: You must be Riya's brother; you look just like her!
Students must not run in the corridor.
quiz.explain: Here 'must' means 'I am almost sure' (a deduction). In the others, 'must' gives a rule or duty.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice that 'must' has two uses: duty and deduction

quiz.q: 'Mummy isn't answering the phone. She ___ be driving.' Choose the best modal for a possibility.
quiz.explain: 'Could' shows one possible reason, which fits when we are not sure.
quiz.mistake: Chooses a negative modal for a possibility

teach.ask: Gappu sees an empty seed bowl and seed shells near his brother. Which words help him show how sure he is about who ate the seeds?
teach.praise: Wow! 'Must' when almost sure, 'might' or 'could' when possible, and 'can't' when almost sure it's not true. Detective Gappu!
teach.nudge: Which modal shows you are almost sure? Which one shows it's only possible? Which shows it's impossible?
